6.0.s.en: (1) The Midianites humiliate the children of Israel

6.0.0.en: In this chapter and the two following chapters the story is repeated of the people of God turning away from Him, then the Midianites humiliating them and their crying out to God, so He sent them Gideon as judge and deliverer. So it is with a person: when God gives him rest, it is natural for him to thank Him, but if he grows slack in his life with God, he is exposed to falling into the sin that humbles him.

6.0.1.en: Midian: they are the descendants of Keturah, the wife of Abraham, and they lived east of the Gulf of Aqaba and north of it as far as the Dead Sea and east of the Jordan River, and the father-in-law of Moses was of them. They cooperated with the Moabites against the children of Israel in the days of Balaam the son of Beor, but Moses defeated them and destroyed them.

6.0.2.en: The children of Israel did evil by turning away from the law of the Lord and from His worship to the worship of idols, so the Lord allowed them to be delivered into the hand of Midian for discipline for a period of seven years.

6.1.0.en: The Midianites oppressed Israel and tightened their grip upon them harshly. Because of the Midianites' attacks upon them, they dug caves for themselves in the mountains to take refuge in during the Midianite raids, and they also dug dens in the mountains in which to hide their crops and livestock lest the Midianites seize them, and they built strongholds to shelter in.

6.2.0.en: The Amalekites: those living in the wilderness of Sinai, whom Moses fought (Ex 17). The children of the east: those living east of the Jordan and east of the Red Sea, among them the Moabites and the sons of Ammon. The Amalekites and the children of the east joined in plundering the children of Israel, attacking them and going up to the mountains where the children of Israel hid their crops and made their caves and dens, in order to seize those crops, and even coming down to them in the plains and valleys, uprooting and destroying the crops, ruining everything in their path from the Jordan River in the east to Gaza in the far west of the land, and plundering even the cattle, sheep and donkeys, leaving nothing good for the subdued people to live on.

6.3.0.en: They did not attack the land of Israel with men only, but brought their cattle with them to graze in the fields of the children of Israel, and also brought their tents to settle in their lands. They came in very great numbers, they and their camels, which devoured the plants as they pleased, so ruin came upon the land after they had exhausted all its good things.

6.4.0.en: Thus disgrace and humiliation came upon the people of Israel because of the oppression of those pagan peoples, and when the matter became very hard for them, they cried out to the Lord, repenting of having left Him and expressing the depth of their need for His mercy and help.

6.4.1.en: Examine yourself, lest your afflictions be because of your distance from God and His forsaking you, so that the devil gains dominion over you and troubles you. And if you discover that, return quickly to Him in repentance, for He is a tender Father who will not leave you.

6.5.s.en: (2) A prophet rebukes the people of God

6.5.0.en: The Lord, who always awaits the return of His children to Him in repentance and the seeking of deliverance, answers them and does not leave them in their perplexity, but sent a prophet to reveal to them the cause of their humiliation, reminding them of His merciful works toward them, which they had met with ingratitude and disobedience. Therefore He delivers them to affliction and discipline so that they may come to themselves and know the measure of their rebellion, their disobedience and their offense against the Lord, and so resolve to repent and return to Him.

6.5.1.en: The prophet begins his speech by stressing that the words he is about to say to them are a message from God. He reminds them that He is the Lord who delivered them from slavery in Egypt and brought them out from there, and rescued them from the Egyptians and from all their oppressions, and led them to the new land He gave them, together with the accompanying miracles of the parting of the Red Sea by the hand of Moses and the victories they achieved with the Lord's help over the original inhabitants of the land and their driving out before them. Perhaps this prophet was Phinehas the son of Eleazar, the son of Aaron the priest.

6.6.0.en: The prophet reminded them that God had reassured them so that they would not fear the pagans and their gods, however strong they appeared, after they had seen God's victories by their hands, and sadly they mingled with the pagans and worshiped their gods, and the pagans humiliated them.

6.6.1.en: Remember God's former works with you so that you may be reassured and trust in God and keep away from everything. Thank Him every day, and your confidence in yourself and your steadfastness in Him will increase.

6.7.0.en: Ophrah: it lies next to Bethel in the western portion of the tribe of Manasseh.

6.7.1.en: Gideon was sitting under a tree in his town of Ophrah, where his clan lived, the clan of the Abiezrites, one of the clans of the tribe of Manasseh. The Lord sent an angel to him to commission him to work at delivering the children of Israel from the slavery of the Midianites. This Gideon was the son of Joash, who was called the Abiezrite because he was of the clan of Abiezer. Gideon was beating wheat with a staff to get the grain out of the ears, and he was doing that inside the winepress so as not to attract the attention of the Midianites, who were watching the Jews to rob them of their good things.

6.8.0.en: The angel appeared to Gideon and began with a greeting, praying that the Lord would help him in the great work with which He would commission him, praising him as the strong man of resolve, to encourage him to undertake the task that would be entrusted to him.

6.9.0.en: Gideon replies and asks the angel with the freedom of love, inquiring that if God is with the children of Israel, why does His people not enjoy the Lord's protection, and why does the Lord not surround them with His care as He did with the previous generations and brought them out of the land of Egypt and rescued them from slavery. But now the Lord is angry with them and has delivered them to their enemies the Midianites, who have gained dominion over them.

6.10.0.en: Here it appears from the inspired text, and from the original word that is translated here as the Lord, which in the Hebrew text is "Yahweh", that the appearance of the Lord in the form of a man was one of the manifestations of the hypostasis of the Son. And the Lord said to him that by this holy zeal of his He would work with him and deliver Israel by his hand. So let him not hesitate, for God sent him and consequently it is He who will give him the victory.

6.11.0.en: Gideon mentions that he is a simple person belonging to a humble clan among the clans of Manasseh, and that he is the youngest among his brothers, so how, being an ordinary man, neither a chief nor a leader among his people, would he be able to gather fighters from the people around him and lead them in a war of liberation. Although he was distinguished by courage, he was humble, and humility is an essential condition for God to work with power in a person.

6.12.0.en: The Lord gives him the decisive answer to his question, which is that it is enough for him that He will be with him, for if the Lord is with a person no power can stand before him. And He assured him that he would defeat the Midianites and should not fear their great number, for he would destroy them as if he were destroying one man only.

6.12.1.en: Do not be troubled by your weakness and do not compare yourself with those who are stronger than you in any capabilities, because God is with you, and as long as God is with you, you will be able to overcome the wars of Satan and achieve every success.

6.13.0.en: The situation was perplexing for Gideon, for he knew perfectly well that he had none of the elements of strength in war, such as military equipment, organization of fighters and the wisdom of military leaders, while the Lord urged him to do the work. Therefore he asked a sign of the Lord to remove his doubts and perplexity. This shows that, besides his courage and humility, he had faith in the power of God able to work in him, but he needed signs to increase and confirm his faith.

6.14.0.en: Gideon asked the Lord not to depart from his place until he came to Him with an offering of food. Gideon's thought was that if He ate of it he would know that He was an ordinary man, and if some divine miracle happened he would realize that He was the Lord. Here God is longsuffering with human weakness, and promised him that He would remain until he returned with his offering. Here appears Gideon's simplicity, which gave him freedom before God, so he spoke with Him as a man speaks with his friend, just as Moses the prophet used to speak with God, and God's humility and fatherhood made Him accept Gideon's words and request and wait for him until he came with an offering to confirm his faith by seeing God.

6.14.1.en: God loves you and rejoices in your friendship with Him, so speak with Him as a son with his father and as a bride with her bridegroom... Express your feelings to Him, for He rejoices in your longings and upholds you and grants you an inexpressible joy.

6.15.1.en: Gideon went into his house and killed a kid of the goats and cooked it, and made unleavened cakes of flour in a large quantity sufficient for ten persons. He prepared this abundant amount to honor the guest. And he put the meat in a basket and the broth in a pot and went out to present it to the wondrous guest.

6.16.0.en: The Lord asked him to lay the meat and the unleavened cakes upon the rock and to pour out the broth over them, to confirm the miracle that was about to take place. Gideon obeyed and did as the Lord commanded him, and by this the rock becomes like an altar on which this offering is presented to God.

6.17.0.en: The Lord put forth the staff, which travelers usually carry, and touched the offering with its end, and fire came out of the rock and consumed the offering, despite the liquids that had been poured over the offering and had drenched it, which would normally extinguish the fire. Then the Lord suddenly vanished from his sight.

6.18.0.en: When Gideon saw the fire come out of the rock and the disappearance of the person who had spoken to him, he realized that he was the angel of the Lord or God Himself, so he was afraid and began to pray, asking mercy from the Lord, because he believed that a man dies if he sees the Lord, as the Lord had declared before to Moses, that man shall not see Him and live (Ex 33:20).

6.19.0.en: God spoke to Gideon a second time, either by a voice or by the appearance of an angel to him or in some other way, and reassured him, giving him the peace that carries the meaning of security and rest, removing all fear from him, because it is He who qualifies him to see Him without dying.

6.20.0.en: Jehovah (Yahweh): the name of God, and its meaning is God is, or He who is.

6.20.2.en: Gideon was reassured and expressed his thanks to God, so he built an altar in the very place where the conversation between him and the Lord took place, that is, beside the terebinth, and called the altar "The Lord is peace" in remembrance of the peace the Lord gave him. And the altar still stands to this day, that is, to the day this book was written, in the city of the Abiezrites, which is Ophrah.

6.20.3.en: It should be noted that Gideon was not of the tribe of Levi, so he had no right to offer sacrifices according to the Law, and he did not offer them in the tabernacle of meeting in Shiloh. But the offering of the sacrifice here is an exceptional matter, the purpose of which is to declare allegiance to God and His worship, and not to Baal, but to despise the worship of idols by using the wood of the grove to kindle the fire for offering the sacrifice (vv. 25, 26).

6.21.s.en: (5) The throwing down of the altar of Baal

6.21.0.en: Baal: a famous pagan god among the Moabites.

6.21.1.en: Grove (pillar): a wooden pillar set up for the pagan gods.

6.21.2.en: God commanded Gideon to take the bullock that his father owned and another bullock seven years old and to throw down with them the altar of Baal and its grove that stood beside it, that is, to remove the worship of idols into which his father and his clan had fallen, and so they provoked God, and He allowed the Midianites to humiliate them. And the second bullock was seven years old as a reminder to them that God feels their suffering during these seven years in which the Midianites humiliated them.

6.22.0.en: Likewise the Lord asked him to build an altar to the Lord, the true God, in a high and visible place as a declaration of the glory of the Lord, and that the building be orderly, to befit the dignity of the Lord. Then He commanded him to offer the second bullock as a burnt offering to the Lord, taking the wood of the grove which he had previously cut down (v. 25) as fuel on the altar of the Lord.

6.23.0.en: Since he was afraid of his brothers and relatives and the people of the city, he decided to carry out secretly at night what the Lord had asked of him, so that no one would obstruct his way. And he took ten men of his servants to help in throwing down the altar of Baal, cutting down the grove, building the new altar for the Lord and offering the burnt offering.

6.23.1.en: Gideon's completing the work by night is a kind of wisdom, so that the work would not be hindered, but it was not out of fear for his life, because they would know it in the morning and could then kill him if God allowed them to. It appears from this that Gideon lived among his family who worshiped idols, but he was not zealous for the worship of idols, as is shown by his immediate obedience to God and his clan's conclusion, when they saw the demolished altar, that it must have been by the hand of Gideon, because they knew his neglect of their pagan worship (v. 29). It should be noted that the offering of the burnt offering here was not on the altar that was in the tabernacle of meeting, and that exception was because of the appearing of God in this place, as happened with David in the threshing floor of Araunah the Jebusite (2 Sam 24:16, 25).

6.24.0.en: When the people of the city rose early, as was their custom, they were surprised to find the altar of Baal thrown down and the grove beside it cut down, and they were astonished at the building of a new altar in its place on which the sacrifice of the second bullock had been offered.

6.25.0.en: The people of the city began to ask, with astonishment and anger, who had committed this deed, wicked in their eyes, so they searched and inquired and finally learned that Gideon was the one who had done it.

6.26.0.en: Immediately they pronounced a swift sentence of death on Gideon, and asked Joash his father to hand him over to them at once so that they might carry out the death sentence on him, as a recompense for the offense he had committed in their eyes by throwing down the altar of Baal and cutting down the grove, which they considered an insult to their god and a defiance of their beliefs.

6.27.0.en: Joash rose to defend what his son had done, since he realized the inability of those false gods to defend themselves, and said to all who were gathered around him: Will you, human beings, contend for Baal, whom you consider a god, or will you save him from the hand of my son, who threw down his altar? If Baal is truly a god, let him defend himself. Then he threatened them that whoever tried to kill his son in defense of Baal, he and the people of his house would fight him at once.

6.28.0.en: Jerubbaal: that is, let Baal fight.

6.28.1.en: From that day Joash gave his son the title "he who fights Baal", saying that if Gideon had assaulted the dignity of Baal by throwing down his altar, let Baal avenge himself. He said that in mockery and contempt of him, because he was certain of Baal's inability to avenge himself on his son Gideon.

6.28.2.en: Be obedient to God however difficult His commandments appear and however contrary to the thoughts of those around you, and be sure that God will give you courage and support you in the face of other people's anger against you.

6.29.s.en: (6) The gathering of soldiers and the two signs of the fleece

6.29.0.en: The valley of Jezreel: a valley in the middle of the land of Palestine extending from the Jordan River to the Mediterranean Sea at Mount Carmel, and because it lies in the middle of the land of Canaan many battles took place in it. The Amalekites and the children of the east joined the Midianites and gathered in the valley of Jezreel to attack the Jews.

6.30.0.en: The Spirit of the Lord came upon him (clothed him): the Spirit of God descended upon him.

6.30.1.en: Gideon was filled with strength and zeal to fight the Midianites when the Spirit of God came upon him, so he blew the trumpet to gather soldiers, and first his clan, the Abiezrites, gathered around him.

6.31.0.en: Gideon was encouraged by the swift change in his clan, which, after demanding his blood, had become the first to answer his call to gather for battle, so he sent messengers to other tribes, Asher, Zebulun and Naphtali, in addition to his own tribe, the tribe of Manasseh. He called these tribes because their dwelling was near him. It should be noted that the tribe of Asher had failed to take part in the war in the days of Deborah and Barak (ch. 5:17), but now it is zealous and joins Gideon in the war. So a person can learn from his failure and put right his state with God by repentance and take part in the spiritual striving, and so have victory over Satan.

6.32.0.en: The floor: the threshing floor, the place where the grain is gathered after its harvest.

6.32.1.en: Gideon asked a sign of the Lord to be sure that He would be with him in his war against the Midianites.

6.32.2.en: The sign Gideon asked for was that he would put a piece of wool on the floor, and if the dew fell in the morning on the piece of wool alone and wet it while the ground of the whole floor was dry, he would be sure by this that the deliverance of Israel would be by his hand. This was a second sign Gideon asked for, because he had first asked of the angel the acceptance of his offering as a sign (vv. 17-21).

6.33.0.en: A bowl: a vessel of clay.

6.33.1.en: Early the next day he went to the floor to see the result, and found the piece of wool wet with water, so he wrung it out and filled a medium-sized vessel with the water.

6.34.0.en: Gideon was not content with the first sign, so he asked the Lord for a second sign, the opposite of the first, so that he would find the piece of wool completely dry while the dew covered all the ground around it; and he besought the Lord not to be angry with him for repeating his requests.

6.35.0.en: The Lord answered Gideon and gave him what he wanted by a great miracle, for on the morning of the next day he found the piece of wool completely dry while the ground around it was covered with water.

6.35.1.en: Here appears God's longsuffering with His children who are weak in faith, for Gideon asked two signs with the fleece, in addition to the angel's acceptance of his offering. God does not hate the weak, but encourages them and upholds them, and even gives additional signs and encouragements, as we shall see in the next chapter.

6.35.2.en: Do not doubt because of your weakness, for God is ready to support you... Ask Him for all your needs and be earnest with Him because He is a tender Father. But be obedient to His commandments and you will find your rest.
